question: What is the main goal of delivering an electrical shock during defibrillation?

options.A: To reset chaotic heart muscle activity and let a normal rhythm restart
options.B: To restart a completely flatlined heart during asystole
options.C: To force the heart valves to open and close manually
options.D: To speed up a dangerously slow resting heart rate

explanation: Think of the shock as a quick reset button! It momentarily stops the heart's chaotic electrical signals all at once, giving the natural pacemaker a chance to step back in and start a normal rhythm. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h1)

question: Which of these heart rhythms needs an immediate emergency shock?
explanation: Ventricular Fibrillation (VF) is a shockable rhythm because the heart still has wild electrical activity that a shock can clear. Flatlines (asystole) need chest compressions and meds, not shocks! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h1)

question: What happens to the heart muscle fibers during Ventricular Fibrillation?

options.A: They beat together in a slow, steady rhythm
options.B: They rest without any electrical signals at all
options.C: They become completely stiff and cannot relax
options.D: They twitch randomly without pumping any blood

explanation: During VF, the heart muscle fibers flutter and twitch chaotically like a bag of worms. Because they aren't working together, no blood is pumped to the body. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h2)

question: Why does Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia lead to cardiac arrest?

options.A: The ventricles beat so fast they cannot fill and empty properly
options.B: The heart muscle grows too thick to receive oxygen
options.C: The electrical signals stop traveling through the atria completely
options.D: The coronary arteries experience a sudden physical blockage

explanation: When the heart races way too fast, it's like trying to fill a bucket with a firehose while the opening is tiny—there's simply no time for blood to fill the chambers, causing a sudden drop in pulse. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h2)

question: How does electricity move through the heart in a biphasic defibrillator?

options.A: It circles around the heart chambers in a clockwise pattern
options.B: It travels forward through the heart and then reverses direction
options.C: It splits into multiple smaller pulses sent simultaneously
options.D: It flows in a single direction from the apex to the base

explanation: Biphasic means two phases! The current travels through the heart in one direction and then quickly switches and flows back through, making it super effective. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h3)

question: What is a big clinical plus of using biphasic defibrillators over monophasic ones?

options.A: They automatically treat both shockable and non-shockable rhythms
options.B: They achieve success with lower energy levels and less tissue injury
options.C: They do not require any conductive gel pads on the chest
options.D: They can deliver shocks safely through wet clothing

explanation: Because biphasic shocks work so well, we don't need as much electricity. This keeps the patient safer by lowering the risk of skin burns and heart muscle damage. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h3)

question: Why must oxygen delivery tubing be moved away before delivering a shock?

options.A: To keep the plastic tubing from melting onto the chest skin
options.B: To allow space for placing the defibrillator pads correctly
options.C: To stop the patient from breathing too much room air
options.D: To prevent electrical sparks from igniting an oxygen-rich fire

explanation: Oxygen feeds fire! Combining an electrical spark from a defibrillator pad with a high concentration of oxygen right near the chest is a major fire hazard. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h4)

question: Where should you place defibrillator pads on a patient with an implanted pacemaker?

options.A: Cover the pacemaker site entirely with thick rubber insulation
options.B: Apply the pads to the upper back and neck instead
options.C: Turn the pacemaker off using an external magnet first
options.D: Place the pads at least one inch away from the pacemaker device

explanation: Always keep the pads at least an inch away from metal devices like pacemakers. Placing them right on top can ruin the device and block the shock from reaching the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h4)

question: What is the first thing a nurse should do right after a shock is delivered?

options.B: Administer a routine dose of IV atropine
options.C: Draw blood samples for arterial blood gas analysis
options.D: Check the carotid pulse for up to one minute

explanation: Don't pause to check for a pulse immediately! Modern resuscitation rules tell us to jump right back into chest compressions to keep blood flowing. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h5)

question: You are getting ready to shock with a manual defibrillator. What is the right sequence right before pressing the discharge button?

options.A: Charge the machine, announce 'clear', and visually check the team
options.B: Pause compressions, check the pulse, and apply gel pads
options.C: Administer emergency epinephrine and remove oxygen tubing
options.D: Turn off the mechanical ventilator and disconnect all IV lines

explanation: Safety first! Always charge the machine, shout a loud 'clear!', and double-check with your eyes that nobody is touching the patient before you hit that button. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h5)

question: Which of these details must a nurse document after an emergency defibrillation?

options.A: Number of shocks delivered and energy levels used
options.B: The specific room temperature during the code
options.C: The patient's personal family medical history
options.D: The exact brand and serial number of the defibrillator

explanation: Good documentation captures the vital facts of the event: how many shocks were given, the energy levels in Joules, and any rhythm changes. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h6)

question: Why is continuous heart monitoring a must right after a successful defibrillation?

options.A: To ensure the patient stays awake during recovery
options.B: To verify that the defibrillator battery is still fully charged
options.C: To measure the exact electrical resistance of the skin
options.D: To catch early warning signs of recurrent arrhythmias or re-arrest

explanation: Just because the heart restarted doesn't mean they're out of the woods. These patients are very fragile and can easily slip right back into a dangerous rhythm. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h6)

question: What usually causes a 'Check Pads' error message to pop up on a defibrillator screen?

options.A: Poor skin contact or loose cable connections
options.B: The patient has an implanted cardiac pacemaker
options.C: The room oxygen level is dangerously high
options.D: The battery is completely charged to maximum capacity

explanation: A 'Check Pads' warning simply means the machine isn't sensing a clean electrical connection with the skin. Check your leads and pad placement! [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h7)

question: Why should a nurse quickly check the patient in person when the monitor shows a sudden weird rhythm?

options.A: To determine if the patient needs an immediate dose of insulin
options.B: To calculate the exact cardiac output of the ventricles
options.C: To check if the intravenous line has become infiltrated
options.D: To rule out artifact caused by movement or loose cables

explanation: Always treat the patient, not just the monitor screen! Shivering, moving around, or a loose cable can make the screen look terrifying even when the patient is totally fine. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T17#GNS213_U1_T17_h7)
